title: THE CHARACTER I ALMOST OVERLOOKED: EPAPHRAS
paragraphs: THE CHARACTER I ALMOST OVERLOOKED: EPAPHRAS
Some names in the Bible are famous.

David.
Moses.
Paul.
Peter.
Their stories fill chapters. Their victories and failures shape entire books of Scripture.
But scattered throughout the New Testament are names that appear only briefly… yet carry enormous spiritual weight.
One of those names is Epaphras.
If you read quickly through the letters of Paul, it is easy to miss him. He only appears in a few verses. No long biography. No dramatic miracle story. No recorded sermon.
Just a few sentences.
But those sentences reveal something powerful.
In Colossians 4:12, Paul writes:
Think about that phrase for a moment.
Always wrestling in prayer.
This was not casual prayer.
This was not a quick moment of religious routine.
The word Paul uses carries the idea of struggle, effort, and intense labor. It is the same kind of language used for athletes competing or soldiers fighting.
Epaphras was not just praying occasionally.
He was laboring in prayer.
And he was not doing it for himself.
He was doing it for others.
Paul says Epaphras was praying so that believers would stand mature and complete in the will of God.
That means Epaphras understood something many people forget:
Spiritual growth does not happen by accident.
Faith must be fought for.
Souls must be covered.
Believers must be strengthened.
And sometimes the greatest battles are fought where no one can see them.
Not on stages.
Not in crowds.
But on your knees before God.
Epaphras may not have been the most visible leader in the early church.
But he was one of the most important.
Because while others were preaching publicly, Epaphras was fighting spiritually.
While churches gathered, Epaphras carried their spiritual condition before God.
While believers slept, Epaphras may have been praying for their strength, their protection, and their maturity.
And Paul noticed.
In the very next verse he says:

"For I testify about him that he has worked hard for you."
— Colossians 4:13
Notice something important.
Paul did not say Epaphras had worked hard in front of people.
He said Epaphras had worked hard for people.
There is a difference.
Many people want to work where they can be seen.
But the Kingdom of God also advances through those who are willing to work where only God sees.
Epaphras reminds us of a truth that challenges our modern culture:
Visibility is not the same as impact.
Today we often measure influence by followers, applause, platforms, or recognition.
But heaven measures influence very differently.
Heaven sees the mother praying for her children long after everyone else has gone to sleep.
Heaven sees the father asking God to guide his family.
Heaven sees the quiet believer who carries friends, church members, and lost souls in prayer.
Those people may never trend online.
But their prayers move heaven.
And sometimes the strength of an entire community rests on the shoulders of people who are quietly interceding.
Epaphras is proof that hidden faithfulness is powerful.
He is mentioned again in Philemon 1:23, where Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus.”
That short phrase suggests Epaphras may have even shared in the suffering that came with following Christ and serving the church.
He was not chasing comfort.
He was committed to Christ and committed to people.
Which brings us to an important question.
Who are the Epaphrases around us today?
They may not be the loudest voices in the church.
They may not hold the microphone.
They may not stand on platforms.
But they are carrying people in prayer.
They are fighting battles in the spiritual realm that no one else even knows are happening.
They are praying for prodigal children.
They are praying for struggling marriages.
They are praying for pastors, missionaries, churches, and communities.
They are praying that believers would stand firm in the will of God.
And if we could see the spiritual impact of those prayers, we might realize that some of the most powerful people in the Kingdom are the ones the world never notices.
Epaphras teaches us something the modern church desperately needs to remember:
Intercession is not a small role.
It is not a backup role.
It is not something we do when we cannot do anything else.
Intercession is spiritual warfare.
It is leadership in the unseen realm.
It is love expressed through persistent prayer.
And heaven records every moment of it.
So the next time you feel like your prayers are small…
Remember Epaphras.
The next time you wonder if your quiet faithfulness matters…
Remember Epaphras.
The next time you think leadership only belongs to those in front…
Remember Epaphras.
Because some of the strongest leaders in the Kingdom are not the ones who speak the most.
They are the ones who wrestle in prayer until others stand strong in God.
And the truth is, every church, every family, and every generation desperately needs more people like him.
So here is the question I want to leave with you:
Do you know someone who has been an Epaphras in your life—someone who has quietly covered you in prayer?
